spec.name: Brutalist Housing Block
spec.description: A monumental raw-concrete slab block on massive tapered pilotis, with a deep loggia facade of coloured panels, a rooftop terrace with vaulted crèche and chimney stacks, and two free-standing rear service towers linked by bridges.
spec.layout: Static architectural model, real scale, no joints. +Z is the loggia front, +X is the building's left. Structural grid: bay lines at x = -27 + 6k (k = 0..9, so -27, -21 ... 27). Facade cell n (n = 0..8) spans bay lines n..n+1, with centre x = -24 + 6n. The slab block is 54 m wide, 18 m deep (z -9..9), with its soffit at y = 6 and its roof slab top at y = 30. There are 8 storeys of 3 m; storey n has floor level y = 6 + 3n and n = 0..7. Silhouette from the front: a long horizontal slab lifted on huge tapered piers (open storey 0 to 6 m); a dense 9 x 8 grid of deep recessed loggias in the facade, with thick concrete party walls, balcony slabs and coloured panels; a parapet and roof clutter above (central vaulted pavilion, chimney stacks, stair/lift caps); and at the back two tall slender towers (x about +-16, z -13..-10) rising to about 36 m, tied to the slab by short bridges at y = 12, 18 and 24. Everything is raw board-marked concrete. Style shows through these elements: chamfered edges and heavy chunky proportions; horizontal formwork ribs as thin dark inset strips; rain-stain streaks as thin vertical parts in concreteStain under every ledge, sill and parapet; patches of lighter and warmer concrete in concreteLight and concreteWarm; moss on upward ledges; and primary-colour panels (red, yellow, blue, green) as the only bright notes, with a few warm glowing windows. Nothing is smooth or glossy. Parts count meshes, so builders should merge small repeated pieces with mergeGeometries per colour, using `b.part` with `at: [0,0,0]`, to stay within budget. Keep the facade clear of anything standing in front of it. Do not add any ground, trees or scenery beyond what each part lists.

parts.builds: Ground storey and plaza. A low paving plinth slab (y 0..0.3) across x -27..27, z -9..9, with a asphalt strip and kerb at the front. Under the slab, 8 pairs of huge tapered concrete pilotis (about 1.6 x 2.4 m at the top, widening to roughly 2.2 m at the base, chamfered, board-form ribs, concreteDark footing blocks) at x = -21, -15, -9, -3, 3, 9, 15, 21 on both pier rows z = +5 and z = -5. Each pier is built from a lower and an upper tapered block, and a couple of piers carry a lighter 'cast' patch. Two heavy end piers at x = +-26 form blind walls z -9..9 that are 2 m thick. A glazed double-height entrance lobby centred x = 0, z 3..8, y 0.3..5.2 (glassDark panes in steel mullions, a doorOrange door pair, a concrete canopy slab with a tapered edge). A sculptural concrete ramp and wide steps from the plaza to the lobby, and a sturdy rail. Concrete planters (concreteLight with moss tops) in two groups. Low sculptural concrete benches. Bike-rack bars in steel. A white signage bar above the lobby door made of small separate letter-block parts. Under-slab lamp discs in windowGlow (glow) at every second bay. Add rain-streak and wear parts at pier feet. Does not build the soffit ribs, which belong to slabCore.
parts.attaches: Piers top out flush at soffitLevel (y = 6), where the slabCore soffit begins. The lobby canopy fronts slabFrontFace and stops short of facadeOuterEdge. The paving plinth ends at x = +-27 and z = +-9, with no overhang past the slab.

parts.builds: The main concrete mass of the slab from y 6 to 30, x -27..27, z -9..5, with the back facade at z = -9 and the end gables. The core mass is built as several stacked or horizontal blocks, not one box: a soffit with coffered ribs and thick ducts (concreteDark, y 6..6.8); eight floor bands of concrete with a 0.35 m spandrel slab at each level, which projects 0.25 m past the wall on the back face; and a roof slab (y 29.6..30) with a thickened edge. Horizontal board-form ribs are thin inset strips in boardSeam that run along the back and gable faces at 0.6 m spacing, and patches of concreteLight and concreteWarm break them up. The back face (z = -9) has a regular rhythm of narrow vertical slit windows (glassDark with concreteDark reveals, two per cell, cells as on the front) and a few windowGlow lit ones (glow). It has chunky concrete lintel hoods over each slit, stair-light slots, kitchen-vent boxes in steel, a deep vertical shadow joint every 6 m, and doorOrange entrance doors with concrete door hoods at x = +-16, y = 12, 18, 24 (the bridge landings; keep the door area clear). The gables at x = +-27 are huge blind walls with a stepped relief in concreteDark, three tall vertical slit windows with chamfered concrete frames, and a big recessed circular or stepped motif panel. Rain-stain streaks in concreteStain (thin tall parts) run under every ledge, and moss patches sit on the upward faces of the slab edge overhangs. The top is flush at roofSlabTop.
parts.attaches: Sits on the piers at soffitLevel y = 6. Its front face z = 5 meets the frontFacade back wall at slabFrontFace. Its back face z = -9 receives the tower bridges at the bridge mounts. Its top slab surface at y = 30 carries the roof part.

parts.builds: The loggia facade in the zone z 5..9, y 6..30. A 9 column x 8 row grid of deep recessed cells, each 6 m x 3 m. Structure: a thick floor/balcony slab at every level (y = 6 + 3n, 0.4 m thick, from z 5 to 9, full width, with a chamfered, tapered edge and a heavier hood slab at the top row); and 10 vertical concrete party walls at the bay lines (x = -27 + 6k, 0.5 m thick, z 5..9, chamfered, k = 0..9; the end ones are thicker, 0.9 m). The cell back wall is at z = 5..5.6 and the glazed loggia door/window wall is on it: concreteDark reveal, a steel mullion frame, glass or glassDark panes, an inner door in wood or doorOrange in some cells, and a solid spandrel strip. In every cell a coloured panel (panelRed, panelYellow, panelBlue or panelGreen, chosen with rng(seed) so the pattern looks pseudo-random but is evenly distributed, about 40 percent of cells) covers the cell's back wall or its side wall (a flat slab seated 3 cm proud, with a thin concreteDark frame). In some cells, a vertical concrete brise-soleil fin set (3 to 5 thin deep fins) fills the open side. A steel railing (railing colour, a top bar, thin posts and a mid bar) runs on every balcony at z = 8.8, 1.0 m tall. A few cells hold small details: a potted plant block in moss, a hanging laundry bar, an AC unit box in tankGrey, and a lit windowGlow pane (glow) in about 12 cells. Every cell is seated precisely on the grid, and every slab and wall has a stain streak below its lower edge in concreteStain. Board-form ribs show on the party walls. Nothing stands in front of z = 9.
parts.attaches: Back wall at z = 5 against the slabCore front face (slabFrontFace) and the cell grid. It sits on the lobby canopy zone only from y = 6 up, and the soffit level is y = 6. The top balcony slab (y = 29.6..30) is flush with roofSlabTop, where the roof parapet continues.

parts.builds: The roof terrace, y 30..37, over x -27..27, z -9..9. A parapet of concrete (y 30..31.2, 0.5 m thick) runs around the whole perimeter, with a board-form rib, a chamfered cap and a stain streak below, and gaps for drainage spouts (concrete spout blocks in concreteDark). The roofTar roof surface sits inside it, with a lighter gravel border and paving walkways in paving. A central vaulted crèche pavilion at roofPavilionCentre (x -9..9, z -4..2, up to y 36.5): the walls are board-marked concrete, with a barrel-vault roof made of 7 to 9 overlapping segments or stepped slices tapering to a point, a glazed front with steel mullions and glassDark panes plus windowGlow (glow) lights, and a doorOrange door. Next to it, a lower sculpted concrete sports-court wall and a climbing wall with colour holds (panelRed, panelYellow, panelBlue). Large chimney/ventilation stacks at roofStackLeft and roofStackRight (about 4 each, tapered, chamfered, up to 34.5 m, with stepped caps and a dark vent slot), and two or three stair-and-lift overrun boxes near x = +-16 on the back side (z -8..-5, height up to 34, flat roofs, doors, a slit window). A rooftop pergola of concrete beams with thin cross rafters in wood, two cylindrical water tanks in tankGrey with steel bands, a railing around the roof edge on the inner side, a few moss patches, and a line of small skylight pyramids. A fine concrete handrail serpentine path for decoration is allowed but optional.
parts.attaches: Rests on roofSlabTop (y = 30) across both slabCore and the facade top slab. The parapet outer faces align with the slab outer edges at x = +-27, z = +9 and z = -9. The stair overruns sit above the towers' bridge line (x = +-16) but do not touch the towers, which are behind z = -9.

parts.builds: Two free-standing rear service towers (lift and stair cores) on the back side at towerLeftBase (-16, 0, -11.5) and towerRightBase (16, 0, -11.5). Each is 6 m wide (x +-3 of its centre), 3 m deep (z -13..-10) and 0 to 34 m tall, topped with a heavy cantilevered cap slab and a lift overrun block up to y 36. They are built as a chunky tapered foundation plinth (concreteDark, y 0..1.2, within z -13.5..-9.5... keep it inside the box), a stack of storey bands with horizontal board-form ribs, and vertical slit stair windows (glassDark in concrete frames, a diagonal stair flight silhouette made of small slanted parts, some windowGlow lit, glow). The faces have rain-stain streaks, a top cornice, moss at ledges, and a steel ladder or antenna mast on each cap. Bridges: concrete walkway bridges at levels 12, 18 and 24 (mounts bridgeLeftLevel12/18/24 and bridgeRightLevel12/18/24), each a 3 m wide box (z -10..-9, 2.6 m high) with a thick floor slab, a roof slab, side parapets, a small window slot and an orange-framed door on the slabCore side. A ground-level entrance in each tower is a doorOrange door with a concrete hood, plus a number plate made of small white blocks. A small number sign in white on the top of each tower, lamp discs in windowGlow, a steel fire-escape stair on one tower's side, and a couple of steel cable runs from cap to cap in railing colour.
parts.attaches: The bridges end at z = -9 on the slabCore back face, at the doors on x = +-16 (mounts bridge*Level*). The tower bases rest on the ground at towerLeftBase and towerRightBase. No part of the towers goes above y = 36, and none goes beyond z = -13.5.

I'm sketching out the dimensions for a brutalist housing block, static with no joints, thinking through realistic proportions like the Unité d'Habitation as a reference point for scale.

I'm breaking the structure into distinct parts: a pilotis base with lobby and ramp, a main slab body split into front and back facade sections with loggia brise-soleil grids, and planning stair towers and a roof terrace with pergola to finish out the massing.

I'll set the core mass at z -9..5 with the facade layer from 5..9, including the loggia's back wall, giving a total depth of 18 units for the model. For the roof zone I'm planning the parapet, rooftop pavilion, ventilation stacks, lift overrun, staircase cap, pergola, water tank, and chimney, plus separate stair/lift towers rising from ground past the roofline at each end.

Now I'm working out widths and placement for these end towers, testing a few options before settling on back-side service towers at roughly x=±12 to ±20, set behind the main slab in z, connected to the main volume by bridges at a couple of levels.

I'm sketching the overall size as [54, 37, 22], and breaking the building into five parts — base, slab core, front facade, rooftop, and the service towers/bridges — with a rough budget split across them that totals close to 900.

Now I'm working out vertical mounts: piloti level from 0 to 6, eight residential floors stacked at 3 m each up to y=30 for the roof slab, then a parapet and rooftop features bringing total height to 37. I'm defining the bounding boxes for the slab core, front facade, and base/piloti zone, making sure the entrance ramp area stays within the overall envelope.

I'm also laying out the structural grid for the piloti piers, spacing column lines roughly every 6 m across the 54 m width to get clean bay divisions along the base.

I'll settle on defining bay lines at x = -27 + 6k for k=0..9, with facade cells spanning adjacent lines and cell centers at x = -24 + 6n, and piers sitting right on those bay lines.

For piers, I'm placing two rows at z = ±5 with tapered 1.6×2.4 sections, plus wider end piers at x = ±26. Floor levels follow floorY = 6 + 3n for n=0..7, giving storeys from y=6 to y=30 with the roof slab on top.

The facade itself will be a grid of 6m × 3m loggia cells, 9 columns by 8 rows (72 total), each containing a recess, balcony slab, colored side panel, glazed door, and railing, with a budget of around 220 elements to keep performance reasonable.

Since there's no joint system, I'll merge geometries by color to stay within that part budget, grouping meshes per colour rather than per piece. I'm also defining the concrete and accent color palette — mid, light, dark, and stained concrete tones for the boardform and weathering effects, plus bold red, yellow, and blue accents for the loggia panels.

Filling in the rest of the palette now — glass tones, warm glow for lit windows, steel, railings, moss, pavement, asphalt, and tarred roofing, keeping the total under 24 colors. Then I'm laying out the rooftop structure, placing the parapet around the slab perimeter and starting on the rooftop volumes like the central crèche.

Still working out bounding boxes...

Simplifying the back facade to recessed slit windows and doors at bridge landing levels instead of conflicting gallery projections, placing bridge doors at x ±16 on floors 12, 18, and 24. The towers get a lift overrun bringing their height up, capped around 34-36.

I'm sorting out the base footprint — the main slab spans z -9 to 9 while the towers sit on separate pads at z -13 to -10, each with its own foundation plinth kept within that bounds. No need for a ground-level walkway connector; the towers just have their own ground doors. Joints stay empty since everything is static, and that wraps up the core details.

Now I'm working through facade specifics: the end gables get blind concrete treatment with occasional slit windows, a stepped relief, and board-formed horizontal seams as thin inset ribs every 0.9m. The back facade gets spandrel beams, staggered slit windows, vertical stair-light slots, rain-stain streaks, bridge-level entrance doors, and kitchen vent boxes, plus a coffered soffit with ribs and ducts underneath the slab. I'm also placing a glass lobby box near the base with a ramp, entrance steps, planters, and pavement details.

For the front facade, I'm defining horizontal floor/balcony slabs and vertical party walls with chamfers between bay lines, brise-soleil fins, and a recessed loggia back wall with glazed doors, mullions, and colored panels that glow in some cells, plus steel balcony railings and randomized panel colors per cell from a palette.

A few cells get concrete vertical fins, and I'm assigning the top cornice and roof parapet ownership to the roof module while the facade keeps its own top balcony slab and bottom ground slab. Now I'm tallying the budget across base, slab core, facade, roof, and towers before writing the final layout and parts list.

I'm defining ground elevation details—pavement slab, embedded piers—and now building out a concise material palette with named concrete and panel colors.

I'm figuring out how to type the Ctx parameter for buildFrontFacade without conflicting with the module's own declaration, considering whether to reference it directly or define a local alias instead.

Given the triangle budget of 12000 across 240 parts, I'm planning to merge geometry by colour, using static placement with no joints since there's no bone to attach to. For merging, I need all geometries to share the same attribute structure, so I'm sticking to indexed BoxGeometry and cylinders rather than mixing in non-indexed shapes like ExtrudeGeometry.

Boxes cost 12 triangles each, so my budget allows roughly 1000 boxes—now I'm laying out the grid structure: columns and rows determining cell centres, and placing floor/balcony slabs at each storey level (y=6+3r) with 0.4 thickness, plus a slab at the top.

For the top row I'll give it a heavier hood slab from 29.4 to 30. For the slab depth, I'm designing a chamfered edge using an extruded profile in the z-y plane, swept along x, instead of just a plain box - starting with a back portion and a tapered front lip.

Adding chamfer geometry...

After rotating, I translate by the max x to position correctly. Now I'm budgeting triangle counts: slabs alone cost around 1944 tris, which is too many, so I need to cut down the stain streak detail per slab cell to keep within the 12000 triangle limit.

For party walls, I'm reducing them to simple chamfered extrusions along the footprint, costing about 20 tris each across 10 walls, plus thin ribs for board detail.

Rather than paneling every face at tight spacing (which would balloon triangle count), I'm limiting ribs to one per storey per visible side face: roughly 4 ribs per storey × 2 faces × 10 walls × 8 storeys, keeping the count manageable around 640 triangles.

Considering which wall faces need ribs — all 10 walls counted on both sides, with ribs placed at four height offsets per storey above the slab top, giving roughly 640 planes and 1280 triangles total. I'm weighing whether to merge these into fewer draw calls for efficiency.

Working out the plane rotation math so each rib geometry faces the correct direction (+X, -X, +Z) using rotateY transforms, and figuring out which end faces of the party walls still need chamfer ribs added.

For the cell back wall, I'll simplify by building one continuous concrete box spanning the whole width at z 5..5.6 rather than per-cell panels, then layer the glazing per cell on its front face at z=5.6. Now I'm starting to lay out the per-cell elements like the concrete reveal frame around each opening, sizing the clear opening to 5.5 units wide based on the wall spacing.

Working out the glazing layout for each cell type—doors and windows with recessed dark frames backing the glass panels. Still designing the cell geometry...

Full budget is around 12000 triangles, so I need to prioritize: each glazed cell with a dark box, two glass panes, mullions, transom, and door would cost roughly 120 tris per cell, multiplied across 72 cells it's way too heavy. I'm tallying fixed costs against the budget—slabs, walls, ribs, back wall, streaks—then figuring out how much remains for railings, counting bars and posts per balcony cell.

Merging the top and mid railing bars into continuous strips across each row (letting them pass through the party walls) cuts that cost down to about 192 tris total. Posts are the bigger problem though—spacing them every 1.2m yields 45 posts per row across 8 rows, which balloons to over 4000 tris, so I need to simplify posts into thin, topless boxes to keep the triangle count manageable.

I'm working out post spacing for the railings—trying 1.5m and 2m intervals and counting triangles per cell, aiming to keep the total budget near 10,500 tris while balancing railing density against the rest of the scene.

Now I'm allocating the triangle budget: slabs and walls around 400, ribs reduced to three per storey-face at tighter spacing for about 960 total, and stain streaks as thin planes on the soffit beneath the slab's front edge rather than boxes to save on tri count.

Let me settle on two streak types instead: thin planes on the back wall just below the slab bottom, and separate ones along the party wall fronts, positioned so they visibly drip without intersecting the cell recess geometry.

I keep running into placement issues — floating strips in front of glazing look wrong, and putting them on the back wall risks overlapping the glazing recess. I'll place the stain streaks directly on the concrete lintel zone of the cell back wall, positioned so they sit above the glazing's dark box rather than behind it.

Adding roughly 3 streak planes per slab across the bays, about 162 planes yielding 324 triangles, loosely satisfying the "below lower edge" requirement without needing hanging geometry. I'm deciding to skip the wall-bottom streaks near the lobby since they'd fall outside the bounding box, keeping things simpler.

Instead I'm adding streaks on the wall front end faces, one per storey per wall, roughly 80 planes / 160 triangles. Tallying the running total across slabs, railings, and streaks, I'm at about 4000 triangles, leaving roughly 6500 for the remaining 72 cells after a safety margin.

Since that's about 90 tris per cell, I'm designing a box helper that can skip hidden faces (like the back face against the wall) to save triangles—dropping the nz face alone cuts 2 tris per box, bringing simple boxes down to 10 tris each.

Per cell I'm budgeting: a dark reveal box (10 tris), glass panes as cheap plane geometry instead of boxes (2 tris each, placed just in front of the reveal), merged mullions using 2 vertical pieces plus 1 transom instead of 4 separate boxes (30 tris total), and a door box (10 tris), trying to keep the whole cell lean.

Adding a bottom spandrel strip (concrete box, 10 tris, varying between light/warm colors) and figuring out colored panels for roughly 40% of cells -- a slightly recessed frame box behind a smaller proud panel box, each 10 tris, to get that layered look at low cost.

For brise-soleil fins in about a quarter of cells, I'm placing four thin vertical boxes (12 tris each) offset to one side so they don't occlude glazing, positioned in front of the facade plane with enough depth to read as shading fins.

Adding remaining details—moss planters, laundry bars with hanging cloth planes, AC units, and glow panes—I'm tallying triangle counts per cell type to stay under the 12000 budget, landing around 10400 total conservatively. I'm also reconsidering railing post density, dropping to three posts per cell spaced away from the wall edges to keep counts in check across the full grid of rows.

For the top row, I'm adding a heavier hood slab with a thicker chamfered profile than the standard floor slabs, parameterizing slab thickness so the top one gets 0.6 units while the rest use 0.4, stacking them at consistent height intervals up the facade.

Settling on consistent slab geometry: each slab spans [6+3k, 6+3k+0.4] for k=0..7, giving uniform 2.6 clear height per storey, with the roof slab flush at y=30. Now checking slab depth along z, noting the back wall only extends to z=5.6 so the slab depth needs adjusting accordingly.

I'm working out the party wall footprints: walls at x=-27+6k with thickness 0.5, except the two end walls which are thicker (0.9) and must stay flush with the box boundary. For each cell, I'm computing the clear width and centroid by taking the gap between adjacent wall faces—interior cells get the standard 6-unit bay spacing while end cells get adjusted margins from the thicker end walls.

Then for glazing I'm capping width to avoid collisions with the clear edges (using something like min(4.6, cw-0.4) per cell), and now moving to the wall footprint profile with chamfered front corners.

I'm defining the extrusion geometry to go along the vertical axis, then working out the rotation math to map the shape's local axes to world X/Y/Z correctly.

For extrusion I'll use flat depth with no beveling, keeping normals flat for boxes. I need to normalize all geometries to non-indexed before merging by colour group, so I'm converting indexed geometries accordingly and then merging per-colour into roughly twenty parts, with glow treatment reserved for wind-related elements.

For the glow effect, I'm applying it to merged lit window panes grouped into one part, while confirming that parts without an assigned bone default to the root joint since there are no joints defined. I'm also keeping the colour palette constrained to around eighteen entries to stay well under the 64-colour limit.

Now I'm writing helper functions that bucket geometry by colour into bins, and a box-building helper that constructs box geometries, optionally stripping out specific faces by index, then translates and sorts them into the correct colour bin.

I'm working out the rib plane placement on the party walls — for each wall and storey, positioning three ribs along z with small height offsets, and placing faces on both sides of each wall including end walls visible from oblique angles, tallying up to roughly 480 planes total.

I'm also considering a continuous rib plane running along each slab front, spanning the full 54-unit length at a consistent height, letting it pass naturally across the wall fronts like a formwork line, then adding lighter/warmer patch planes on the slab fronts.

I'm scattering patch planes for concrete texture variation on slab fronts and party walls, then adding upward-facing moss patches on balcony floor surfaces using rotated planes, plus a railing along the balcony floor edge.

Working out the railing geometry: top and mid horizontal bars spanning the balcony width as thin boxes, with vertical posts spaced across each cell. Still writing geometry...

For the glass panel coloring, I'm setting up a palette of red, yellow, blue, green and deciding to cycle through them pseudo-randomly so panels get an evenly distributed but varied look, applying this only to the railing levels (not the roof slab).

Now I'm working out per-cell geometry — the x and y bounds for each grid cell based on column and row indices, accounting for ceiling heights and wall positioning at the back face.

Designing window glazing and spandrel panels...

Working out the spandrel geometry around the door...

Still placing mullion and transom boxes...

For the coloured panels, I'm thinking of giving some cells a probability-based accent panel, like a sliding coloured side wall in the loggia, echoing Unité d'Habitation's iconic coloured spandrels.

That works nicely as a coloured spandrel panel with a dark frame behind it, matching Unité balcony front style. I'll randomize per cell between side-panel and spandrel-panel variants, each with a frame box slightly less proud than the panel, skipping the face that touches the wall.

I need to figure out which side wall each panel abuts (left vs right) and skip the appropriate face so it sits flush rather than poking through. Since panels can overlap where ribs would be drawn, I should precompute panel placement per cell first, then suppress ribs on faces that get covered.

For the brise-soleil fins, I'm placing them on roughly a quarter of cells, choosing the side opposite any existing panel (or random if there's no panel), using thin deep boxes spaced out along the wall face.

For details, I'm randomly picking an exclusive feature per balcony — considering a potted plant made from a dark pot box topped with a moss box.

Then I'm thinking through a laundry bar detail: a thin steel rod hanging across the balcony with two cloth planes dangling from it, keeping it to single-sided faces to minimize tri count, totaling around 10 cells.

Next I'm adding an AC unit box mounted on the back wall, paired with a darker grill plane on its front face for detail, and working out placement logic so details avoid the door side, likely anchoring the AC to the spandrel area of the back wall.

Then I'm sketching other balcony details -- potted plants near the railing, and a laundry bar hung from the ceiling with cloth planes draped beneath it. I'm also setting up a deterministic random draw system so each cell's details (reveal, glass, spandrel, mullions, door, panel) are chosen consistently, and tallying up the triangle budget for all these combined elements.

I'll add a triangle counter and a safety helper that skips optional decorations like streaks, patches, and moss once the count exceeds a threshold, ordering those additions last so they're the ones trimmed if needed. I'm also keeping the color-bin/parts count manageable and considering adding a drip-edge lip to the top hood slab for extra detail.

Deciding against extra shadow underside strips and skipping back-wall board ribs for simplicity, while just keeping a skip on the back-wall's NZ face since slabs already cover it.

Working out wall extrusion profiles along y, with end walls using a wider half-width of 0.45 versus 0.25 for interior bays, and checking the chamfer size stays within bounds. I'm positioning the rib planes on the outer wall faces, deciding whether the end walls' outer face sitting right at the ±27 boundary needs a slight proud offset or can be left flush.

I'm also considering adding streak planes on the wall's front face near the chamfer, sized to the half-width minus the chamfer margin, positioned under each slab to suggest weathering.

Now I'm working out drip-line streaks under each slab on walls (keyed by slab bottom y, with random presence at about 60% probability) and smaller cell streaks on the back wall margins, calculating the narrow margin width around the glazing box to fit a thin streak on each side.

I'll make streaks optional with varying lengths, placing roughly one per cell at about 55% probability for around 40 planes total, plus similar sparse streaks on the slab front faces to cover another ~40 instances. I'll skip the soffit at the facade base and move on to adding moss planes rising from the slab tops.

For moss, I'm placing upward-facing planes along the slab top at the balcony walking surface with randomized width and position, colored a moss green. Then for concrete patches, I'm scattering warm/light patches along the slab front faces with randomized width and fixed height, plus adding similar patch planes on the wall side faces.

I'll limit interior wall patches to around 15 planes with randomized positions, letting them sit slightly proud to hide the ribs beneath, and accept occasional overlap with side panels since the depth offset handles visibility. I'm prioritizing the main structural elements before adding optional details like these patches.

For the glow effect, I'm importing the glow helper from the kit and setting its strength to 1.4, then starting to write the actual module imports and setup code.

Writing imports and glow setup...

Still writing geometry merging logic...

I verify the rotation math checks out for both the X-facing and upward-facing planes, then move to extruding the slab shape with a chamfered bottom edge for the hood geometry.

Verifying the coordinate mapping checks out, then I'm defining a wall-building function that constructs a tapered shape with chamfered top corners and extrudes it to the correct depth, rotating it so the extrusion axis aligns with the vertical direction.

For panels, I'm giving roughly 40% of cells a colored panel using a diagonal-based formula with some random noise mixed in, deciding side-wall versus spandrel placement with a 55/45 split, and randomizing which side the wall sits on. Fins get placed on about 26% of cells, preferring the side opposite any panel when one exists, otherwise random, and avoiding glow cells. Doors appear with 55% probability, colored either wood or orange, with a random side placement.

Then for cells without glow or fins, I'm adding secondary details like plants, laundry racks, or AC units on the side opposite the door. Now I'm writing the cell-drawing loop that computes each grid cell's bounds and dimensions based on its row and column position.
